templates.title: Find and classify critical points (second derivative test)

variants.problem: Find all critical points of $f(x,y)=- x^{3} + 9 x y - y^{3}$ and classify each as a local maximum, local minimum or saddle point.
variants.solution:
$f_x=- 3 x^{2} + 9 y$ and $f_y=9 x - 3 y^{2}$. Solving $f_x=f_y=0$ gives the critical points $(0,0)$, $(3,3)$.

Second derivatives: $f_{xx}=- 6 x$, $f_{yy}=- 6 y$, $f_{xy}=9$, and $D=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2$:

point$f_{xx}$$f_{yy}$$f_{xy}$$D$type
$(0,0)$$0$$0$$9$$-81$saddle point
$(3,3)$$-18$$-18$$9$$243$local maximum

($D<0$: saddle point; $D>0$ and $f_{xx}>0$: local minimum; $D>0$ and $f_{xx}<0$: local maximum.)

variants.problem: A particle moves along $\vec r(t)=\langle 3 t,\ \frac{1}{t},\ 2 t^{2}\rangle$. Find the tangential and normal components of its acceleration at $t=1$.

$\vec v=\langle 3,\ - \frac{1}{t^{2}},\ 4 t\rangle$ and $\vec a=\langle 0,\ \frac{2}{t^{3}},\ 4\rangle$. At $t=1$: $\vec v=\langle 3,\ -1,\ 4\rangle$, $\vec a=\langle 0,\ 2,\ 4\rangle$, $|\vec v|=\sqrt{26}$.

\[a_T=\frac{\vec v\cdot\vec a}{|\vec v|}=\frac{14}{\sqrt{26}}=\frac{7 \sqrt{26}}{13}.\]

$\vec v\times\vec a=\langle -12,\ -12,\ 6\rangle$, so

\[a_N=\frac{|\vec v\times\vec a|}{|\vec v|}=\frac{18}{\sqrt{26}}=\frac{9 \sqrt{26}}{13}.\]

Check: $a_T^2+a_N^2=|\vec a|^2=20$.

templates.title: Mass of a plate over a region between two curves

variants.problem: A thin plate occupies the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$ and $(0,2)$ and has density $\delta(x,y)=x^{2}$. Find its mass.
variants.solution:
The slanted side is $y=2 - 2 x$, so the triangle is $0\le x\le1$, $0\le y\le2 - 2 x$.

\[m=\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{2 - 2 x}x^{2}\,dy\,dx.\]

Inner integral (in $y$): $- 2 x^{3} + 2 x^{2}$.

\[m=\int_{0}^{1}\left(- 2 x^{3} + 2 x^{2}\right)dx=\frac{1}{6}.\]

variants.problem: A thin plate occupies the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(2,0)$ and $(0,1)$ and has density $\delta(x,y)=x y$. Find its mass.
variants.solution:
The slanted side is $y=1 - \frac{x}{2}$, so the triangle is $0\le x\le2$, $0\le y\le1 - \frac{x}{2}$.

\[m=\int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^{1 - \frac{x}{2}}x y\,dy\,dx.\]

Inner integral (in $y$): $\frac{x^{3}}{8} - \frac{x^{2}}{2} + \frac{x}{2}$.

\[m=\int_{0}^{2}\left(\frac{x^{3}}{8} - \frac{x^{2}}{2} + \frac{x}{2}\right)dx=\frac{1}{6}.\]

variants.problem: A thin plate occupies the region between $y=x^2$ and $y=4 x$ and has density $\delta(x,y)=2 y$. Find its mass.
variants.solution:
The curves meet where $x^2=4 x$: $x=0$ and $x=4$. Between them $y=4 x$ is on top.

\[m=\int_{0}^{4}\int_{x^{2}}^{4 x}2 y\,dy\,dx.\]

Inner integral (in $y$): $- x^{4} + 16 x^{2}$.

\[m=\int_{0}^{4}\left(- x^{4} + 16 x^{2}\right)dx=\frac{2048}{15}.\]

variants.problem: Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of $f(x,y)=x^{2} + 2 x y - 3 x - y^{2} - 3 y$ on the rectangle $0\le x\le3$, $0\le y\le3$.
variants.solution:
Interior. $f_x=2 x + 2 y - 3$ and $f_y=2 x - 2 y - 3$. Setting both to zero gives no critical point strictly inside the region.

Boundary. Parametrize each edge and find the critical points of the one-variable function:

  • From $(0,0)$ to $(3,0)$: $f=9 t^{2} - 9 t$ for $0\le t\le1$; critical at $t=\frac{1}{2}$.
  • From $(3,0)$ to $(3,3)$: $f=- 9 t^{2} + 9 t$ for $0\le t\le1$; critical at $t=\frac{1}{2}$.
  • From $(0,3)$ to $(3,3)$: $f=9 t^{2} + 9 t - 18$ for $0\le t\le1$; no critical point inside.
  • From $(0,0)$ to $(0,3)$: $f=- 9 t^{2} - 9 t$ for $0\le t\le1$; no critical point inside.

Compare every candidate, including the corners:

templates.title: Partial derivatives of z defined implicitly

variants.problem: The equation $2 x y z - x z^{2} - 2 z^{3}=1$ defines $z$ as a function of $x$ and $y$ near the point $(-1,-1,1)$. Find $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}$ and $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}$ at that point.
variants.solution:
Let $F(x,y,z)=2 x y z - x z^{2} - 2 z^{3} - 1$. Implicit differentiation gives $z_x=-\dfrac{F_x}{F_z}$ and $z_y=-\dfrac{F_y}{F_z}$.

$F_x=2 y z - z^{2}$, $F_y=2 x z$, $F_z=2 x y - 2 x z - 6 z^{2}$. At $(-1,-1,1)$: $F_x=-3$, $F_y=-2$, $F_z=-2$.

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\frac{-3}{-2}=- \frac{3}{2},\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\frac{-2}{-2}=-1.\]

variants.problem: The equation $- 3 x^{2} y - x e^{z + 1} + 3 z^{3}=-3$ defines $z$ as a function of $x$ and $y$ near the point $(0,1,-1)$. Find $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}$ and $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}$ at that point.
variants.solution:
Let $F(x,y,z)=- 3 x^{2} y - x e^{z + 1} + 3 z^{3} + 3$. Implicit differentiation gives $z_x=-\dfrac{F_x}{F_z}$ and $z_y=-\dfrac{F_y}{F_z}$.

$F_x=- 6 x y - e^{z + 1}$, $F_y=- 3 x^{2}$, $F_z=- x e^{z + 1} + 9 z^{2}$. At $(0,1,-1)$: $F_x=-1$, $F_y=0$, $F_z=9$.

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\frac{-1}{9}=\frac{1}{9},\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\frac{0}{9}=0.\]

variants.problem: The equation $2 x^{2} y - 3 x y z - y^{2} z=4$ defines $z$ as a function of $x$ and $y$ near the point $(0,2,-1)$. Find $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}$ and $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}$ at that point.
variants.solution:
Let $F(x,y,z)=2 x^{2} y - 3 x y z - y^{2} z - 4$. Implicit differentiation gives $z_x=-\dfrac{F_x}{F_z}$ and $z_y=-\dfrac{F_y}{F_z}$.

$F_x=4 x y - 3 y z$, $F_y=2 x^{2} - 3 x z - 2 y z$, $F_z=- 3 x y - y^{2}$. At $(0,2,-1)$: $F_x=6$, $F_y=4$, $F_z=-4$.

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\frac{6}{-4}=\frac{3}{2},\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\frac{4}{-4}=1.\]

variants.problem: The equation $x^{2} z - x y z + 2 x e^{z - 2}=8$ defines $z$ as a function of $x$ and $y$ near the point $(2,1,2)$. Find $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}$ and $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}$ at that point.
variants.solution:
Let $F(x,y,z)=x^{2} z - x y z + 2 x e^{z - 2} - 8$. Implicit differentiation gives $z_x=-\dfrac{F_x}{F_z}$ and $z_y=-\dfrac{F_y}{F_z}$.

$F_x=2 x z - y z + 2 e^{z - 2}$, $F_y=- x z$, $F_z=x^{2} - x y + 2 x e^{z - 2}$. At $(2,1,2)$: $F_x=8$, $F_y=-4$, $F_z=6$.

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\frac{8}{6}=- \frac{4}{3},\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\frac{-4}{6}=\frac{2}{3}.\]

variants.problem: The equation $- 3 x z^{2} - x e^{z + 1} + y z^{3}=2$ defines $z$ as a function of $x$ and $y$ near the point $(0,-2,-1)$. Find $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}$ and $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}$ at that point.
variants.solution:
Let $F(x,y,z)=- 3 x z^{2} - x e^{z + 1} + y z^{3} - 2$. Implicit differentiation gives $z_x=-\dfrac{F_x}{F_z}$ and $z_y=-\dfrac{F_y}{F_z}$.

$F_x=- 3 z^{2} - e^{z + 1}$, $F_y=z^{3}$, $F_z=- 6 x z - x e^{z + 1} + 3 y z^{2}$. At $(0,-2,-1)$: $F_x=-4$, $F_y=-1$, $F_z=-6$.

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\frac{-4}{-6}=- \frac{2}{3},\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\frac{-1}{-6}=- \frac{1}{6}.\]

variants.problem: The equation $3 x z^{2} + x e^{z - 1} + 2 z^{3}=-2$ defines $z$ as a function of $x$ and $y$ near the point $(-1,2,1)$. Find $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}$ and $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}$ at that point.
variants.solution:
Let $F(x,y,z)=3 x z^{2} + x e^{z - 1} + 2 z^{3} + 2$. Implicit differentiation gives $z_x=-\dfrac{F_x}{F_z}$ and $z_y=-\dfrac{F_y}{F_z}$.

$F_x=3 z^{2} + e^{z - 1}$, $F_y=0$, $F_z=6 x z + x e^{z - 1} + 6 z^{2}$. At $(-1,2,1)$: $F_x=4$, $F_y=0$, $F_z=-1$.

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\frac{4}{-1}=4,\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\frac{0}{-1}=0.\]

variants.problem: The equation $- 3 x z^{2} + 3 y^{2} z - 3 z^{3}=0$ defines $z$ as a function of $x$ and $y$ near the point $(0,-1,1)$. Find $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}$ and $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}$ at that point.
variants.solution:
Let $F(x,y,z)=- 3 x z^{2} + 3 y^{2} z - 3 z^{3}$. Implicit differentiation gives $z_x=-\dfrac{F_x}{F_z}$ and $z_y=-\dfrac{F_y}{F_z}$.

$F_x=- 3 z^{2}$, $F_y=6 y z$, $F_z=- 6 x z + 3 y^{2} - 9 z^{2}$. At $(0,-1,1)$: $F_x=-3$, $F_y=-6$, $F_z=-6$.

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\frac{-3}{-6}=- \frac{1}{2},\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\frac{-6}{-6}=-1.\]

variants.problem: The equation $3 x^{2} z - x y z + 2 y^{2} z=-3$ defines $z$ as a function of $x$ and $y$ near the point $(-1,0,-1)$. Find $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}$ and $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}$ at that point.
variants.solution:
Let $F(x,y,z)=3 x^{2} z - x y z + 2 y^{2} z + 3$. Implicit differentiation gives $z_x=-\dfrac{F_x}{F_z}$ and $z_y=-\dfrac{F_y}{F_z}$.

$F_x=6 x z - y z$, $F_y=- x z + 4 y z$, $F_z=3 x^{2} - x y + 2 y^{2}$. At $(-1,0,-1)$: $F_x=6$, $F_y=-1$, $F_z=3$.

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\frac{6}{3}=-2,\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\frac{-1}{3}=\frac{1}{3}.\]

$F_x=2 x y$, $F_y=x^{2} + 6 y z$, $F_z=3 y^{2} + 9 z^{2}$. At $(-2,0,2)$: $F_x=0$, $F_y=4$, $F_z=36$.

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\frac{0}{36}=0,\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\frac{4}{36}=- \frac{1}{9}.\]

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\frac{-16}{27}=\frac{16}{27},\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\frac{-11}{27}=\frac{11}{27}.\]

$F_x=y z + 2 z^{2}$, $F_y=x z - 2 z^{3}$, $F_z=x y + 4 x z - 6 y z^{2}$. At $(-2,-1,2)$: $F_x=6$, $F_y=-20$, $F_z=10$.

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\frac{6}{10}=- \frac{3}{5},\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\frac{-20}{10}=2.\]

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\frac{-1}{4}=\frac{1}{4},\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\frac{18}{4}=- \frac{9}{2}.\]

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\frac{-3}{5}=\frac{3}{5},\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\frac{-1}{5}=\frac{1}{5}.\]

$F_x=- 4 x z - e^{z - 2}$, $F_y=- 6 y z$, $F_z=- 2 x^{2} - x e^{z - 2} - 3 y^{2}$. At $(2,0,2)$: $F_x=-17$, $F_y=0$, $F_z=-10$.

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\frac{-17}{-10}=- \frac{17}{10},\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\frac{0}{-10}=0.\]

variants.problem: The equation $- 3 x z^{2} + x e^{z - 2} + y z^{3}=-8$ defines $z$ as a function of $x$ and $y$ near the point $(0,-1,2)$. Find $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}$ and $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}$ at that point.
variants.solution:
Let $F(x,y,z)=- 3 x z^{2} + x e^{z - 2} + y z^{3} + 8$. Implicit differentiation gives $z_x=-\dfrac{F_x}{F_z}$ and $z_y=-\dfrac{F_y}{F_z}$.

$F_x=- 3 z^{2} + e^{z - 2}$, $F_y=z^{3}$, $F_z=- 6 x z + x e^{z - 2} + 3 y z^{2}$. At $(0,-1,2)$: $F_x=-11$, $F_y=8$, $F_z=-12$.

\[\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\frac{-11}{-12}=- \frac{11}{12},\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\frac{8}{-12}=\frac{2}{3}.\]

variants.solution:
Let $F(x,y,z)=- x e^{z - 1} + y z^{3} + z^{3} - 2$. Implicit differentiation gives $z_x=-\dfrac{F_x}{F_z}$ and $z_y=-\dfrac{F_y}{F_z}$.

variants.problem:
Let $f(x,y)=\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$.

(a) Find the tangent plane to $z=f(x,y)$ at $(6,8)$.
(b) Use it to estimate $f(\frac{59}{10},\frac{79}{10})$.
variants.solution:
(a) $f(6,8)=10$, $f_x=\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}$ and $f_y=\frac{y}{\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}$, so $f_x(6,8)=\frac{3}{5}$ and $f_y(6,8)=\frac{4}{5}$.

\[z=10+\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)(x-6)+\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)(y-8)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z=\frac{3 x}{5} + \frac{4 y}{5}.\]

(b) With $\Delta x=- \frac{1}{10}$ and $\Delta y=- \frac{1}{10}$:

\[f(\frac{59}{10},\frac{79}{10})\approx 10+\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)\left(- \frac{1}{10}\right)+\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)\left(- \frac{1}{10}\right)=\frac{493}{50}\approx 9.8600.\]

templates.title: Bounding the error with Taylor's inequality

variants.problem: Let $T_{2}(x)$ be the degree-$2$ Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=e^{x}$ about $x=0$. Use Taylor's inequality to bound $|f(x)-T_{2}(x)|$ for $x$ in $[-1,\,0]$.
variants.solution:
Taylor's inequality: if $|f^{(3)}(x)|\le M$ on the interval, then $|f(x)-T_{2}(x)|\le\dfrac{M}{(3)!}|x|^{3}$.

$f^{(3)}(x)=1e^{x}$. On $[-1,\,0]$ we have $x\le0$, so $e^{x}\le1$ and $|f^{(3)}(x)|\le1$; take $M=1$. Also $|x|\le1$:

\[|f(x)-T_{2}(x)|\le\frac{1}{3!}\left(1\right)^{3}=\frac{1}{6}\approx0.167.\]

Taylor's inequality: if $|f^{(4)}(x)|\le M$ on the interval, then $|f(x)-T_{3}(x)|\le\dfrac{M}{(4)!}|x|^{4}$.

$f^{(4)}(x)=16e^{2 x}$. On $[-1,\,0]$ we have $2 x\le0$, so $e^{2 x}\le1$ and $|f^{(4)}(x)|\le16$; take $M=16$. Also $|x|\le1$:

\[|f(x)-T_{3}(x)|\le\frac{16}{4!}\left(1\right)^{4}=\frac{2}{3}\approx0.667.\]

templates.title: A Taylor polynomial about a point

variants.problem: Find the Taylor polynomial $T_{3}(x)$ of $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ about $x=1$.
Find the Taylor polynomial $T_{3}(x)$ of $f(x)=\ln{\left(x \right)}$ about $x=2$.
Find the Taylor polynomial $T_{2}(x)$ of $f(x)=\cos{\left(2 x \right)}$ about $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$.
variants.solution:
$T_n(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(x-a)^k$. Derivatives:

  • $f(x)=\cos{\left(2 x \right)}$, so $f(\frac{\pi}{2})=-1$
  • $f^{(1)}(x)=- 2 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}$, so $f^{(1)}(\frac{\pi}{2})=0$
  • $f^{(2)}(x)=- 4 \cos{\left(2 x \right)}$, so $f^{(2)}(\frac{\pi}{2})=4$
\[T_{2}(x)=-1 + \frac{4}{2!}\left(x-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{2}=-1+2\left(x-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{2}.\]

variants.problem: Find the Taylor polynomial $T_{3}(x)$ of $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ about $x=4$.
Find the Taylor polynomial $T_{3}(x)$ of $f(x)=\sin{\left(x \right)}$ about $x=\pi$.
variants.solution:
$T_n(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(x-a)^k$. Derivatives:

  • $f(x)=\sin{\left(x \right)}$, so $f(\pi)=0$
  • $f^{(1)}(x)=\cos{\left(x \right)}$, so $f^{(1)}(\pi)=-1$
  • $f^{(2)}(x)=- \sin{\left(x \right)}$, so $f^{(2)}(\pi)=0$
  • $f^{(3)}(x)=- \cos{\left(x \right)}$, so $f^{(3)}(\pi)=1$
\[T_{3}(x)=\left(-1\right)\left(x-\pi\right) + \frac{1}{3!}\left(x-\pi\right)^{3}=-\left(x-\pi\right)+\frac{1}{6}\left(x-\pi\right)^{3}.\]

variants.problem: Find the Maclaurin series of $f(x)=e^{3 x^{3}}$: write its first four nonzero terms, the series in sigma notation, and its radius of convergence.
variants.solution:
Start from $e^u=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{u^n}{n!}$ and substitute $u=3 x^{3}$:

\[e^{3 x^{3}}=1+3 x^{3}+\frac{9 x^{6}}{2}+\frac{9 x^{9}}{2}+\cdots=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{3^{n} x^{3 n}}{n!}.\]

The series for $e^u$, $\sin u$ and $\cos u$ converge for every $u$, so the radius of convergence is $R=\infty$.

variants.problem: Find the Maclaurin series of $f(x)=\cos{\left(x^{3} \right)}$: write its first four nonzero terms, the series in sigma notation, and its radius of convergence.
variants.solution:
Start from $\cos u=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{(-1)^nu^{2n}}{(2n)!}$ and substitute $u=x^{3}$:

\[\cos{\left(x^{3} \right)}=1- \frac{x^{6}}{2}+\frac{x^{12}}{24}- \frac{x^{18}}{720}+\cdots=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\left(-1\right)^{n} x^{6 n}}{\left(2 n\right)!}.\]

The series for $e^u$, $\sin u$ and $\cos u$ converge for every $u$, so the radius of convergence is $R=\infty$.

The known series converges for $|u|<1$, i.e. $|3 x|<1$, which means $|x|<\frac{1}{3}$. So $R=\frac{1}{3}$.

The series for $e^u$, $\sin u$ and $\cos u$ converge for every $u$, so the radius of convergence is $R=\infty$.

\[\sin{\left(2 x \right)}=2 x- \frac{4 x^{3}}{3}+\frac{4 x^{5}}{15}- \frac{8 x^{7}}{315}+\cdots=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\left(-1\right)^{n} 2^{2 n + 1} x^{2 n + 1}}{\left(2 n + 1\right)!}.\]

The series for $e^u$, $\sin u$ and $\cos u$ converge for every $u$, so the radius of convergence is $R=\infty$.

variants.problem: Find the Maclaurin series of $f(x)=\frac{x^{2}}{x^{3} + 1}$: write its first four nonzero terms, the series in sigma notation, and its radius of convergence.

\[\frac{x^{2}}{x^{3} + 1}=x^{2}- x^{5}+x^{8}- x^{11}+\cdots=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(-1\right)^{n} x^{3 n + 2}.\]

The known series converges for $|u|<1$, i.e. $|x^{3}|<1$, which means $|x|<1$. So $R=1$.

variants.problem: Find the Maclaurin series of $f(x)=\frac{1}{x^{2} + 1}$: write its first four nonzero terms, the series in sigma notation, and its radius of convergence.

\[\frac{1}{x^{2} + 1}=1- x^{2}+x^{4}- x^{6}+\cdots=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(-1\right)^{n} x^{2 n}.\]

The known series converges for $|u|<1$, i.e. $|- x^{2}|<1$, which means $|x|<1$. So $R=1$.

The series for $e^u$, $\sin u$ and $\cos u$ converge for every $u$, so the radius of convergence is $R=\infty$.

templates.title: Parametric equations for the line where two planes meet

variants.problem:
Find parametric equations for the line of intersection of the planes

\[x-y-z=-2\qquad\text{and}\qquad 2x-3y-2z=-6.\]
variants.answer: $x=- t,\quad y=2,\quad z=- t$ (or any equivalent parametrization)
variants.solution:
The line lies in both planes, so it is perpendicular to both normals $\vec n_1=\langle 1,\ -1,\ -1\rangle$ and $\vec n_2=\langle 2,\ -3,\ -2\rangle$. A direction vector is

\[\vec n_1\times\vec n_2=\langle -1,\ 0,\ -1\rangle.\]

For a point on the line, set $z=0$ and solve the two plane equations: $x=0$, $y=2$. So $(0,2,0)$ is on the line, and

\[x=- t,\quad y=2,\quad z=- t.\]

(Any point on the line and any nonzero multiple of the direction give an equally correct answer.)

templates.title: The plane through three points, and the triangle's area

variants.problem:
Let $P(-1,0,-1)$, $Q(0,-2,1)$ and $R(-3,-3,4)$.

(a) Find an equation of the plane through $P$, $Q$ and $R$.
(b) Find the area of triangle $PQR$.
variants.solution:
(a) $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\langle 1,\ -2,\ 2\rangle$ and $\overrightarrow{PR}=\langle -2,\ -3,\ 5\rangle$. A normal vector is

\[\vec n=\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}=\langle -4,\ -9,\ -7\rangle.\]

Using the point $P$: $-4(x+1)-9y-7(z+1)=0$, i.e.

\[-4x-9y-7z=11.\]

(b) The area is half the length of the cross product: $\frac12\left|\langle -4,\ -9,\ -7\rangle\right|=\frac12\sqrt{146}=\frac{\sqrt{146}}{2}$.

variants.solution:
(a) $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\langle 1,\ 2,\ -5\rangle$ and $\overrightarrow{PR}=\langle -1,\ 1,\ -1\rangle$. A normal vector is

\[\vec n=\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}=\langle 3,\ 6,\ 3\rangle\parallel\langle 1,\ 2,\ 1\rangle.\]

Using the point $P$: $1(x+1)+2(y-1)+1(z-3)=0$, i.e.

\[x+2y+z=4.\]

(b) The area is half the length of the cross product: $\frac12\left|\langle 3,\ 6,\ 3\rangle\right|=\frac12\sqrt{54}=\frac{3 \sqrt{6}}{2}$.

(b) The area is half the length of the cross product: $\frac12\left|\langle -20,\ 20,\ -5\rangle\right|=\frac12\sqrt{825}=\frac{5 \sqrt{33}}{2}$.

Let $P(-1,-1,-1)$, $Q(4,-2,1)$ and $R(-1,0,3)$.

(a) Find an equation of the plane through $P$, $Q$ and $R$.
(b) Find the area of triangle $PQR$.
variants.solution:
(a) $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\langle 5,\ -1,\ 2\rangle$ and $\overrightarrow{PR}=\langle 0,\ 1,\ 4\rangle$. A normal vector is

\[\vec n=\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}=\langle -6,\ -20,\ 5\rangle.\]

Using the point $P$: $-6(x+1)-20(y+1)+5(z+1)=0$, i.e.

\[-6x-20y+5z=21.\]

(b) The area is half the length of the cross product: $\frac12\left|\langle -6,\ -20,\ 5\rangle\right|=\frac12\sqrt{461}=\frac{\sqrt{461}}{2}$.
